description: Pilot AL, task 2 (objreply): objection-reply pairs from four real exchanges. Items are built by scripts/philbench_items.objreply(): for each pair, objection->reply (four replies) and reply->objection (four objections), the three distractors drawn from the same exchange, the key's position rotated across A-D; a 'paraphrase' variant repeats every item with all texts paraphrased (memorisation control). Texts are excerpts with OCR and spelling normalised; 'adaptation' notes any further change. 'echo' marks pairs where the reply repeats distinctive words of the objection, so analysis can report them separately. Claude drafted the excerpts and paraphrases; every pair awaits the author's check.

exchanges.edition: Descartes, Philosophical Works, vol. II, trans. Haldane & Ross (1912): Third Set of Objections (Hobbes) with the Author's Reply

pairs.location: Objection IV and Reply, pp. 65-66; source line ~3331
pairs.adaptation: Objection trimmed.
pairs.objection: There is a great difference between imagining, that is, having some idea, and conceiving with the mind, that is, inferring as the result of a train of reasoning that something is or exists. But what shall we now say, if reasoning chance to be nothing more than the uniting and stringing together of names or designations by the word 'is'? It will follow that reason gives us no conclusion about the nature of things, but only about the terms that designate them. Thus reasoning will depend on names, names on the imagination, and imagination, perchance, on the motion of the corporeal organs; and so mind will be nothing but the motions in certain parts of an organic body.
pairs.reply: In reasoning we unite not names but the things signified by the names; and I marvel that the opposite can occur to anyone. For who doubts whether a Frenchman and a German are able to reason in exactly the same way about the same things, though they yet conceive the words in an entirely diverse way? And if my opponent admits that words signify anything, why will he not allow our reasonings to refer to this something that is signified, rather than to the words alone? It will be as correct to infer that earth is heaven as to conclude that mind is motion.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: Imagining, which is having an idea, differs greatly from conceiving with the mind, which is concluding by a chain of reasoning that something is or exists. But suppose reasoning turns out to be no more than joining and linking names or labels with the word 'is'. Then reason would tell us nothing about how things are, only about the words we use for them. Reasoning would rest on names, names on imagination, and imagination perhaps on movements of bodily organs; so the mind would be nothing but movements in certain parts of a living body.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: When we reason we connect not names but the things the names stand for, and I am astonished that anyone could think otherwise. Nobody doubts that a Frenchman and a German can reason identically about the same things, even though the words they have in mind are completely different. And if my critic grants that words mean something, why not grant that our reasoning concerns what they mean rather than the bare words? Concluding that the mind is motion is no better than concluding that the earth is the sky.

pairs.location: Objection V and Reply, pp. 66-68; source line ~3394
pairs.adaptation: Objection trimmed; the blind man and fire illustration omitted. Reply's last sentence on creation omitted.
pairs.objection: When I think of a man, I recognize an idea or image with figure and colour as its constituents. But when one thinks of an Angel, what is noticed in the mind is now the image of a flame, now that of a fair winged child, and this has no likeness to an Angel. It is the same way with the most holy name of God; we have no image, no idea corresponding to it. Hence it appears that we have no idea of God, and a man who reasons back to an eternal cause merely gives a name to the object of his faith or reasoning and calls it God.
pairs.reply: Here the meaning assigned to the term idea is merely that of images depicted in the corporeal imagination; and, that being agreed on, it is easy to prove that there is no proper idea of Angel or of God. But I have everywhere shown that I take the term idea to stand for whatever the mind directly perceives. So when I will or when I fear, since at the same time I perceive that I will and fear, that very volition and apprehension are ranked among my ideas. I employed this term because it was the term currently used by philosophers for the forms of perception of the Divine mind, though we can discover no imagery in God.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: When I think of a man, I find an idea or image made up of shape and colour. But thinking of an angel, what appears in the mind is sometimes a flame and sometimes a handsome child with wings, and neither resembles an angel. The same holds for the most holy name of God: no image or idea answers to it. So it seems we have no idea of God, and someone who reasons back to an eternal cause simply attaches a name to what he believes or infers and calls it God.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: This takes 'idea' to mean only pictures formed in the bodily imagination; grant that, and it is easy to show there is no real idea of an angel or of God. But I have made clear throughout that by 'idea' I mean whatever the mind perceives directly. So when I will or fear, since I perceive at the same time that I am willing and fearing, the willing and the fearing count among my ideas. I chose the word because philosophers already used it for the forms of perception in God's mind, even though there are no images in God.

pairs.location: Objection X (last paragraph) and Reply (last paragraph), pp. 72-73; source line ~3757
pairs.adaptation: Only the paragraphs on innateness are used.
pairs.objection: When M. Descartes says that the idea of God and that of the soul are innate in us, I should like to know whether the minds of those who are in a profound and dreamless sleep yet think. If not, they have at that time no ideas. Whence no idea is innate, for what is innate is always present.
pairs.reply: When I say that an idea is innate in us, or imprinted in our souls by nature, I do not mean that it is always present to us. This would make no idea innate. I mean merely that we possess the faculty of summoning up this idea.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: Descartes says the ideas of God and of the soul are inborn in us; I would like to know whether people in deep, dreamless sleep are still thinking. If they are not, they have no ideas at that moment. So no idea is inborn, since what is inborn is present at all times.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: By calling an idea innate, or stamped on our souls by nature, I do not mean that we are always aware of it. On that reading no idea would be innate. I mean only that we have the ability to call this idea to mind.

pairs.location: Objection XII and Reply, pp. 74-75; source line ~3843
pairs.adaptation: Objection's second paragraph (on free will and the Calvinists) and reply's matching part omitted.
pairs.objection: It is true that ignorance is merely a defect, and that we stand in need of no special positive faculty in order to be ignorant; but about error the case is not so clear. For it appears that stones and inanimate things are unable to err solely because they have no faculty of reasoning or imagining. Hence it is a very direct inference that, in order to err, a faculty of reasoning, or at least of imagination, is required; and both of these are positive faculties.
pairs.reply: Although in order to err the faculty of reasoning, or rather of judging, or affirming and denying, is required, because error is a lack of this power, it does not hence follow that this defect is anything real. Just so it does not follow that blindness is anything real, although stones are not said to be blind merely because they are incapable of vision.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: Granted, ignorance is only a lack, and we need no special positive faculty to be ignorant; but error is a less clear case. For stones and other lifeless things seem unable to make mistakes only because they cannot reason or imagine. So it follows quite directly that making a mistake requires a power of reasoning, or at least of imagining, and both of these are positive powers.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: To err one must indeed have the power of reasoning, or more exactly of judging, of affirming and denying, since error is a failure of that power; but it does not follow that this failure is something real. In the same way blindness is not something real, even though we do not call stones blind just because they cannot see.

pairs.location: Objection XV and Reply, pp. 77-78; source line ~4043
pairs.adaptation: Objection's quotation of Meditation VI omitted.
pairs.objection: It is the common belief that no fault is committed by medical men who deceive sick people for their health's sake, nor by parents who mislead their children for their good. The evil in deception lies not in the falsity of what is said, but in the bad intent of those who practise it. One must therefore examine whether the proposition 'God can in no case deceive us', taken universally, is true; for if it is not, the conclusion that corporeal things exist does not follow.
pairs.reply: For the security of my conclusion we do not need to assume that we can never be deceived, for I have gladly admitted that we are often deceived. We need only assume that we are not deceived when that error of ours would argue an intention to deceive on the part of God, an intention it is contradictory to impute to Him.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: People generally think doctors do nothing wrong when they deceive the sick for the sake of their health, nor parents when they mislead their children for their good. What makes deception wrong is not that something false is said but that the deceiver means harm. So we must ask whether 'God never deceives us in any case' is true as a universal claim; if it is not, it does not follow that bodies exist.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: My conclusion is secure without supposing that we are never deceived; I have readily granted that we often are. It requires only that we are not deceived in cases where our mistake would show that God meant to deceive us, since it is contradictory to ascribe such an intention to Him.

pairs.location: Final Objection and Reply, p. 78; source line ~4089
pairs.adaptation: Objection's quotation of Meditation VI omitted.
pairs.objection: I ask whether it is really the case that one who dreams he doubts whether he dreams or no is unable to dream that his dream is connected with the idea of a long series of past events. If he can, those things which to the dreamer appear to be the actions of his past life may be regarded as true just as though he had been awake. Besides, if all certitude depends on knowing the true God, either an Atheist cannot infer from the memory of his previous life that he wakes, or a man can know that he is awake apart from knowledge of the true God.
pairs.reply: One who dreams cannot effect a real connection between what he dreams and the ideas of past events, though he can dream that he does connect them; and when he has awakened he will easily detect his error. An Atheist is able to infer from the memory of his past life that he is awake. Still he cannot know that this sign is sufficient to give him the certainty that he is not in error, unless he knows that it has been created by a God who does not deceive.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: I ask whether someone who dreams that he is wondering whether he is dreaming really cannot dream that his dream fits into a long history of past events. If he can, then what seem to the dreamer to be the deeds of his past life could be taken as true just as if he were awake. Moreover, if all certainty rests on knowing the true God, then either an atheist cannot conclude from remembering his past life that he is awake, or one can know one is awake without knowing the true God.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: A dreamer cannot actually link what he dreams with his ideas of past events, though he can dream that he links them; and once awake he will easily notice his mistake. An atheist can conclude from remembering his past life that he is awake. But he cannot know that this sign suffices to make him certain he is not mistaken unless he knows it was made by a God who does not deceive.

exchanges.edition: A Collection of Papers which passed between Mr. Leibnitz and Dr. Clarke (London, 1717), Clarke's English translation of Leibniz

pairs.location: Leibniz, First Paper §4; Clarke, First Reply §4; source lines ~818, ~1098
pairs.adaptation: Long s and spelling normalised.
pairs.objection: According to their doctrine, God Almighty wants to wind up his watch from time to time; otherwise it would cease to move. He had not, it seems, sufficient foresight to make it a perpetual motion. Nay, the machine of God's making is so imperfect, according to these gentlemen, that he is obliged to clean it now and then by an extraordinary concourse, and even to mend it, as a clockmaker mends his work; who must consequently be so much the more unskilful a workman, as he is oftener obliged to mend his work and to set it right.
pairs.reply: Among men, an artificer is justly esteemed the more skilful as his machine will continue longer to move regularly without any farther interposition, because the skill of all human artificers consists only in composing or adjusting certain movements whose principles of motion, such as weights and springs, are altogether independent of the artificer. But with regard to God the case is quite different, because he not only composes or puts things together, but is himself the author and continual preserver of their original forces or moving powers. And consequently it is not a diminution, but the true glory of his workmanship, that nothing is done without his continual government and inspection.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: On their view, almighty God has to wind up his watch every so often, or else it would stop. Apparently he lacked the foresight to make it run forever. Worse, these gentlemen make God's machine so imperfect that he must clean it now and then by special intervention, and even repair it as a clockmaker repairs his clock; and the more often a workman has to repair and correct his work, the less skilled he must be.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: Among people, a craftsman is rightly thought more skilled the longer his machine keeps running smoothly without his stepping in again, because human skill lies only in assembling or adjusting parts whose sources of motion, like weights and springs, do not depend on the craftsman at all. With God it is entirely different, since he not only assembles things but himself creates and constantly sustains their basic forces and powers of motion. So it is no lessening but the real glory of his work that nothing happens without his constant rule and oversight.

pairs.location: Leibniz, Third Paper §3; Clarke, Third Reply §3; source lines ~2820, ~3605
pairs.adaptation: Long s and spelling normalised; Clarke's footnotes omitted.
pairs.objection: These gentlemen maintain that space is a real absolute being. But this involves them in great difficulties, for such a being must needs be eternal and infinite. Hence some have believed it to be God himself, or one of his attributes, his immensity. But since space consists of parts, it is not a thing which can belong to God.
pairs.reply: Nor is there any difficulty in what is here alleged about space having parts. For infinite space is one, absolutely and essentially indivisible; and to suppose it parted is a contradiction in terms, because there must be space in the partition itself, which is to suppose it parted and yet not parted at the same time. The immensity or omnipresence of God is no more a dividing of his substance into parts than his duration, or continuance of existing, is a dividing of his existence into parts. There is no difficulty here but what arises from the figurative abuse of the word parts.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: These gentlemen hold that space is a real, absolute being. But that lands them in serious trouble, since such a being would have to be eternal and infinite. That is why some have taken it to be God himself, or one of his attributes, namely his immensity. But space is made up of parts, so it cannot be something that belongs to God.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: The claim that space has parts raises no difficulty either. Infinite space is one and, absolutely and by its nature, indivisible; to suppose it divided is self-contradictory, since there would have to be space in the very gap between the parts, so that it would be divided and undivided at once. God's immensity, or presence everywhere, no more splits his substance into parts than his duration, his going on existing, splits his existence into parts. The only difficulty comes from using the word 'parts' figuratively and wrongly.

pairs.location: Leibniz, Third Paper §4; Clarke, Third Reply §4; source lines ~2830, ~3686
pairs.adaptation: Long s and spelling normalised.
pairs.objection: As for my own opinion, I have said more than once that I hold space to be something merely relative, as time is; that I hold it to be an order of coexistences, as time is an order of successions. For space denotes, in terms of possibility, an order of things which exist at the same time, considered as existing together, without enquiring into their manner of existing. And when many things are seen together, one perceives that order of things among themselves.
pairs.reply: If space was nothing but the order of things coexisting, it would follow that if God should remove in a straight line the whole material world entire, with any swiftness whatsoever, yet it would still always continue in the same place, and that nothing would receive any shock upon the most sudden stopping of that motion. And if time was nothing but the order of succession of created things, it would follow that if God had created the world millions of ages sooner than he did, yet it would not have been created at all the sooner. Further, space and time are quantities, which situation and order are not.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: My own view, as I have said several times, is that space is something purely relative, just as time is: space is an order of things existing together, as time is an order of things following one another. For space signifies, as a matter of possibility, an order among things that exist at once, taken as existing together, without asking how they exist. And when we see many things together, we perceive this order among them.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: Were space only the order of things existing together, then if God moved the entire material world along a straight line at any speed at all, it would still remain in the same place, and nothing would feel any jolt if that motion were stopped abruptly. And were time only the order in which created things succeed one another, then had God created the world millions of ages earlier than he did, it would not have been created any earlier at all. Besides, space and time are quantities, and position and order are not.

pairs.location: Leibniz, Third Paper §5; Clarke, Third Reply §5 (with the last sentence from §2); source lines ~2890, ~3712
pairs.adaptation: Long s and spelling normalised; Leibniz trimmed. The reply's last sentence is from Clarke's §2, where he states the same point.
pairs.objection: Space is something absolutely uniform; and, without the things placed in it, one point of space does not absolutely differ in any respect whatsoever from another point of space. Now from hence it follows, supposing space to be something in itself besides the order of bodies among themselves, that it is impossible there should be a reason why God, preserving the same situations of bodies among themselves, should have placed them in space after one certain particular manner and not otherwise; why everything was not placed the quite contrary way, for instance, by changing east into west. But if space is nothing else but that order or relation, then those two states would not at all differ from one another, and there is no room to enquire after a reason of the preference of the one to the other.
pairs.reply: The uniformity of space does indeed prove that there could be no external reason why God should create things in one place rather than in another. But does that hinder his own will from being to itself a sufficient reason of acting in any place, when all places are indifferent or alike, and there be good reason to act in some place? In things in their own nature indifferent, mere will, without anything external to influence it, is alone that sufficient reason.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: Space is completely uniform: leaving aside the things in it, no point of space differs in any way at all from any other point. It follows, if space is something in its own right over and above the arrangement of bodies among themselves, that there could be no reason why God, keeping the bodies' positions relative to each other the same, put them in space in this particular way rather than another, for example with east and west swapped. But if space is nothing but that arrangement or relation, the two states would not differ at all, and there is no reason to look for to explain choosing one over the other.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: The sameness of space does show that there could be no outside reason for God to create things in one place rather than another. But does that stop his own will from being a sufficient reason by itself for acting in some place, when all places are equal and alike and there is good reason to act somewhere? Where things are by nature indifferent, will alone, with nothing outside it moving it, is the sufficient reason.

pairs.location: Leibniz, Fourth Paper §4; Clarke, Fourth Reply §§3-4; source lines ~4352, ~5559
pairs.adaptation: Long s and spelling normalised; Clarke's argument about solid particles omitted.
pairs.objection: There is no such thing as two individuals indiscernible from each other. An ingenious gentleman of my acquaintance, discoursing with me in the presence of the Princess Sophia in the garden of Herrenhausen, thought he could find two leaves perfectly alike. The princess defied him to do it, and he ran all over the garden a long time to look for some, but it was to no purpose. Two drops of water, or milk, viewed with a microscope, will appear distinguishable from each other; and this is an argument against atoms.
pairs.reply: It is very true that no two leaves, and perhaps no two drops of water, are exactly alike, because they are bodies very much compounded. But the case is very different in the parts of simple solid matter. And even in compounds, there is no impossibility for God to make two drops of water exactly alike. And if he should make them exactly alike, yet they would never the more become one and the same drop of water because they were alike.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: No two individual things are ever indistinguishable from one another. A clever gentleman I know, talking with me before Princess Sophia in the gardens at Herrenhausen, believed he could find two leaves exactly alike. The princess challenged him to do so, and he searched the whole garden for a long time without success. Look at two drops of water or of milk under a microscope and you will be able to tell them apart; and this tells against atoms.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: It is quite right that no two leaves, and perhaps no two drops of water, are exactly the same, since they are highly composite bodies. But the parts of simple solid matter are a very different case. And even among composite things, nothing prevents God from making two drops of water exactly alike. And if he did, their being alike would not in the least make them one and the same drop.

exchanges.edition: Gaunilo, In Behalf of the Fool, and Anselm's Apologetic, trans. S. N. Deane (Open Court, 1903)

pairs.location: Gaunilo §2; Anselm, Apologetic ch. VI; source lines ~7548, ~8314
pairs.adaptation: Both trimmed.
pairs.objection: This being is said to be in my understanding already, only because I understand what is said. Could it not with equal justice be said that I have in my understanding all manner of unreal objects, having absolutely no existence in themselves, because I understand these things if one speaks of them, whatever they may be? Unless indeed it is shown that this being is of such a character that it cannot be held in concept like all unreal objects, or objects whose existence is uncertain.
pairs.reply: I was attempting to prove what was still uncertain, and contented myself at first with showing that this being is understood in any way, and is in the understanding. It was my intention to consider, on these grounds, whether this being is in the understanding alone, like an unreal object, or whether it also exists in fact, as a real being. For if unreal objects, or objects whose existence is uncertain, are in this way understood and in the understanding, there is no reason why that being of which I spoke should not be understood and be in the understanding.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: This being is said to be in my understanding already just because I understand what is said about it. But could one not say just as fairly that every sort of unreal thing, with no existence of its own, is in my understanding, since I understand such things whenever someone talks of them? Unless it is shown that this being is of a kind that cannot be held in thought the way unreal things, or things of doubtful existence, are held.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: I was trying to prove something not yet settled, and at first I was content to show only that this being is understood in some way and is in the understanding. From there I meant to ask whether it is in the understanding only, like something unreal, or also exists in fact, as something real. For if unreal things, or things of doubtful existence, are understood and in the understanding in this way, nothing prevents the being I spoke of from being understood and in the understanding.

pairs.location: Gaunilo §3; Anselm, Apologetic ch. VIII (first part); source lines ~7603, ~8417
pairs.adaptation: Gaunilo trimmed (Augustine's joiner omitted).
pairs.objection: Your example of the painter who already has in his understanding what he is to paint cannot agree with this argument. For the picture, before it is made, is contained in the artificer's art itself; and any such thing, existing in the art of an artificer, is nothing but a part of his understanding itself. Hence, even if it were true that there is a being than which a greater is inconceivable, yet to this being, when heard of and understood, the not yet created picture in the mind of the painter is not analogous.
pairs.reply: Your so careful demonstration that the being than which a greater cannot be conceived is not analogous to the not yet executed picture in the understanding of the painter is quite unnecessary. It was not for this purpose that I suggested the preconceived picture. I had no thought of asserting that the being which I was discussing is of such a nature; but I wished to show that what is not understood to exist can be in the understanding.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: Your example of the painter, who already has in mind what he is going to paint, does not fit this argument. Before the picture is made, it is contained in the craftsman's skill itself, and anything that exists in a craftsman's skill is simply part of his own understanding. So even if there were a being than which no greater can be conceived, the unpainted picture in the painter's mind would not be comparable to that being as heard of and understood.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: You go to great pains to show that the being than which no greater can be conceived is not like the unpainted picture in the painter's mind, but there was no need. That is not why I mentioned the picture planned in advance. I never meant to claim that the being I was discussing is of that kind; I only wanted to show that something not understood to exist can be in the understanding.

pairs.location: Gaunilo §4; Anselm, Apologetic ch. VIII (second part); source lines ~7633, ~8440
pairs.adaptation: Both trimmed; Gaunilo's illustration of the unknown man omitted, Anselm's ascending series of goods omitted.
pairs.objection: So far as actual knowledge of the object, either from its specific or general character, is concerned, I am as little able to conceive of this being when I hear of it, or to have it in my understanding, as I am to conceive of or understand God himself. For I do not know that reality itself which God is, nor can I form a conjecture of that reality from some other like reality; for you yourself assert that that reality is such that there can be nothing else like it. Of God, or a being greater than all others, I could not conceive at all, except merely according to the word.
pairs.reply: Obviously this is not true. For everything that is less good, in so far as it is good, is like the greater good. It is therefore evident to any rational mind that by ascending from the lesser good to the greater, we can form a considerable notion of a being than which a greater is inconceivable. There is, then, a means of forming a notion of a being than which a greater is inconceivable.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: As far as real knowledge of the thing goes, whether of its species or its genus, I can no more conceive of this being when I hear of it, or hold it in my understanding, than I can conceive of or understand God himself. I do not know the reality that God is, and I cannot guess at it from some similar reality, since you yourself say that nothing else can be like it. So I could not conceive of God, or of a being greater than all others, at all, except by the word alone.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: This is plainly false. Whatever is less good resembles the greater good insofar as it is good. So any rational mind can see that, by rising from lesser goods to greater ones, we can form a substantial notion of a being than which no greater can be conceived. There is, therefore, a way to form a notion of a being than which no greater can be conceived.

pairs.location: Gaunilo §6; Anselm, Apologetic ch. III; source lines ~7746, ~8057
pairs.adaptation: Both trimmed.
pairs.objection: It is said that somewhere in the ocean is an island which, because of the impossibility of discovering what does not exist, is called the lost island, and that it is more excellent than all other countries in the abundance of its riches. Now suppose someone went on to say, as if by a logical inference: you can no longer doubt that this island exists somewhere, since you have no doubt that it is in your understanding; and since it is more excellent to exist both in the understanding and in reality, for this reason it must exist. If a man should try to prove to me by such reasoning that this island truly exists, either I should believe that he was jesting, or I know not which I ought to regard as the greater fool: myself, supposing that I should allow this proof, or him.
pairs.reply: I promise confidently that if any man shall devise anything existing either in reality or in concept alone, except that than which a greater cannot be conceived, to which he can adapt the sequence of my reasoning, I will discover that thing, and will give him his lost island, not to be lost again. But it now appears that this being than which a greater is inconceivable cannot be conceived not to be, because it exists on so assured a ground of truth. For if it could be conceived not to exist, it could be conceived to have a beginning and an end; but this is impossible.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: People say there is an island somewhere in the ocean, called the lost island because what does not exist cannot be found, and that it surpasses every other land in the wealth of its riches. Now suppose someone added, as though drawing a logical conclusion: you can no longer doubt that this island exists somewhere, since you do not doubt it is in your understanding; and since existing in reality as well as in the understanding is more excellent, it must exist. If anyone tried to prove to me in this way that the island really exists, I would either think he was joking, or not know which of us was the bigger fool: me, if I accepted the proof, or him.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: I promise with confidence that if anyone can think up anything at all, existing in reality or only in thought, other than that than which no greater can be conceived, to which my line of reasoning can be applied, I will find that thing and give him his lost island, never to be lost again. But it is now clear that this being than which no greater can be conceived cannot be conceived not to exist, since it exists on so secure a footing of truth. For if it could be conceived not to exist, it could be conceived to begin and to end, and that is impossible.

pairs.location: Gaunilo §7; Anselm, Apologetic ch. IV; source lines ~7788, ~8108
pairs.adaptation: Both trimmed.
pairs.objection: It is said that the non-existence of this being is inconceivable. It might better be said, perhaps, that its non-existence, or the possibility of its non-existence, is unintelligible, for according to the true meaning of the word, unreal objects are unintelligible. I am most certainly aware of my own existence; but I know, nevertheless, that my non-existence is possible. Whether, so long as I am most positively aware of my existence, I can conceive of my non-existence, I am not sure; but if I cannot, God will not be the only being of which it can be said that it is impossible to conceive of his non-existence.
pairs.reply: It was more proper to say it cannot be conceived. For although no objects which exist can be understood not to exist, yet all objects, except that which exists in the highest degree, can be conceived not to exist. For all those objects, and those alone, can be conceived not to exist, which have a beginning or end or composition of parts. Be assured, then, that you can conceive of your own non-existence, although you are most certain that you exist.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: We are told that this being's non-existence cannot be conceived. Perhaps it would be better to say that its non-existence, or the possibility of its non-existence, cannot be understood, since strictly speaking what is unreal cannot be understood. I am entirely certain that I exist, yet I know that I could fail to exist. Whether I can conceive of my non-existence while I am fully certain of my existence, I do not know; but if I cannot, then God will not be the only being whose non-existence is said to be inconceivable.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: 'Cannot be conceived' was the right expression. For while nothing that exists can be understood not to exist, everything except what exists in the highest degree can be conceived not to exist. Precisely those things, and only those, can be conceived not to exist that have a beginning, an end, or parts. So rest assured that you can conceive of yourself not existing, even though you are entirely certain that you exist.

exchanges.edition: Vitoria, De Indis et De Jure Belli Relectiones, trans. J. P. Bate (Carnegie, 1917): arguments Vitoria reports and his answers to them

pairs.location: De Indis, Sect. I, §4 (argument) and §24 (answer), pp. 120, 128; source lines ~6109, ~6765
pairs.adaptation: Argument trimmed; its description of the Indians as 'little different from brute animals' omitted. Answer trimmed.
pairs.objection: Slaves own no property, for a slave can have nothing of his own. But the aborigines in question are slaves; for as Aristotle says, some are by nature slaves, those, to wit, who are better fitted to serve than to rule, who have not sufficient reason to govern even themselves, but only to do what they are bidden. And Aristotle says it is just and natural for such to be slaves. Therefore they and their like cannot be owners.
pairs.reply: Aristotle certainly did not mean that such as are not over-strong mentally are by nature subject to another's power and incapable of dominion over themselves and other things; for this is civil and legal slavery, wherein none are slaves by nature. Nor does he mean that, if any by nature are of weak mind, it is permissible to seize their patrimony and enslave them; but that by defect of their nature they need to be ruled and governed by others, just as sons need to be subject to their parents until of full age. Accordingly, even if we admit that they are as inept as is alleged, still dominion cannot be denied to them.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: A slave owns nothing, since a slave can have nothing of his own. But these native peoples are slaves; for Aristotle says some people are slaves by nature, namely those better suited to serving than to ruling, who lack enough reason to govern even themselves and can only follow orders. And Aristotle says it is just and natural for such people to be slaves. So neither they nor others like them can be owners.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: Aristotle surely did not mean that people of limited intelligence are by nature under another's power and unable to own themselves or anything else; that is civil, legal slavery, and nobody is a slave of that kind by nature. Nor did he mean that, if some are naturally weak-minded, one may take their inheritance and enslave them; he meant that through a natural deficiency they need others to rule and guide them, as children must obey their parents until they come of age. So even granting that they are as incapable as is claimed, they cannot be denied dominion.

pairs.location: De Jure Belli, §38 (Doubt I), pp. 179-180; source line ~10740
pairs.adaptation: The Deuteronomy argument is split off into its own pair (vit-deuteronomy).
pairs.objection: It seems lawful to slay guiltless youths of the enemy when they may be expected to cause danger in the future, on the same principle which justifies the incidental killing of other guiltless persons. For the children of Saracens are guiltless, but there is good reason to fear that when grown up they will fight against Christians; and the adult male civilians of the enemy, though presumed innocent, will hereafter carry a soldier's arms and cause the same hazard.
pairs.reply: Although this killing may possibly be defended, I believe that it is in no wise right, seeing that evil is not to be done even in order to avoid greater evil still, and it is intolerable that anyone should be killed for a future fault. There are, moreover, other available measures of precaution against their future conduct, namely, captivity, exile, and the like.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: It appears permissible to kill innocent young enemies who are likely to pose a danger later, on the same principle that permits the incidental killing of other innocent people. The Saracens' children are innocent, but there is good reason to fear they will fight Christians once grown; and the enemy's adult men who are not soldiers, though presumed innocent, will later take up arms and pose the same danger.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: Though a defence of such killing might be attempted, I hold that it is entirely wrong, since evil must not be done even to prevent a greater evil, and it is intolerable to kill anyone for a wrong not yet committed. Besides, there are other ways to guard against what they may do later, such as captivity, exile and the like.

pairs.location: De Jure Belli, §38 (Doubt I), p. 180; source line ~10755
pairs.adaptation: The argument's conclusion (sentence 3) is made explicit; in the text it is implied by 'Now, is it lawful to slay these?'. Author: check.
pairs.objection: When assaulting any city, the Sons of Israel were ordered to slay every adult male, as is written in Deuteronomy, chapter 20. Now, it cannot be presumed that all of these would be guilty. It is therefore lawful in war to slay the adult males of the enemy, although they are not shown to be guilty.
pairs.reply: The slaughter in the instances named was at the special command of God, who was wroth against the people in question and wished to destroy them utterly, just as he sent fire on Sodom and Gomorrah which devoured both guiltless and guilty together. He, however, is Lord of all and has not given this license as a common law.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: In Deuteronomy, chapter 20, the Israelites were commanded to kill every grown man whenever they attacked a city. Yet one cannot assume that every one of these men was guilty. So in war it is permissible to kill the enemy's grown men even when their guilt has not been shown.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: In the cases mentioned, the killing happened by God's special command, because he was angry with those peoples and meant to wipe them out entirely, as when he sent fire on Sodom and Gomorrah that consumed the innocent and the guilty alike. But he is Lord of all, and he did not grant this permission as a general law.

pairs.location: De Indis, Sect. I, §6, p. 121-122; source line ~6218
pairs.adaptation: Almain's argument restated from Vitoria's report; its conclusion (sentence 3) made explicit.
pairs.objection: A person already in mortal sin who finds himself in extreme need would, if sin took away his dominion, be in a dilemma, inasmuch as he must eat bread, and if he cannot own any himself he takes another's. Therefore he could not escape mortal sin. Hence it cannot be that mortal sin deprives a man of dominion.
pairs.reply: This reasoning is unsatisfactory: in the first place, because neither Armachanus nor Wycliffe seems to be speaking of natural dominion, but of civil. Secondly, the consequence is denied, it being retorted that in case of necessity a man could take what is another's. And thirdly, he is in no dilemma, because he can repent.
pairs.objection_paraphrase: Someone already in mortal sin who falls into extreme need would, if sin removed his dominion, face a dilemma: he has to eat bread, and if he cannot own any himself, he must take someone else's. So he could not avoid mortal sin. Therefore mortal sin cannot strip a person of dominion.
pairs.reply_paraphrase: This argument does not work. First, neither Armachanus nor Wycliffe appears to be talking about natural dominion, only civil. Second, the inference is rejected, with the answer that in necessity a person may take what belongs to another. Third, there is no dilemma, since he is able to repent.
